Zyrardow Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Żyrardów, Poland

Not demolished. NOTE: the source page's description field for this record was found to duplicate the unrelated Mszczonów Jewish Cemetery entry word-for-word, so that text is not used here; the account below comes from independent research instead. Żyrardów itself was founded in the 1830s as a linen-mill town, named for its French factory director Philippe de Girard, and its Jewish community grew rapidly from about 70 to 3,000 residents through the late 19th century, concentrated in a district along today's Mireckiego and Szulmana Streets. In 1874, authorities permitted the formal establishment of a Jewish religious community, and Count Feliks Sobański donated land for both a synagogue and this cemetery. During World War II, the cemetery itself became a site of German executions - victims reportedly included a woman named Miller and her three-year-old child, along with Dawid Funtowicz, killed for attempting to smuggle food into the Warsaw Ghetto. The Nazis also used uprooted tombstones to pave streets and courtyards. A Holocaust memorial obelisk, erected in 1967, bears plaques honoring both Żyrardów's victims and Samuel Meppen, credited with helping rebuild the cemetery after the war.
